items.title: Genetics & Genetic Engineering — the toolkit
items.body:
### Genetics and the genetic-engineering toolkit

**In one line**
Genetic engineering means deliberately changing an organism's DNA, and it is done with a small set of "molecular tools" — scissors, glue, carriers and a photocopier for DNA.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC loves "match the tool to its job" and "which statement is correct" items on restriction enzymes, ligase, vectors, PCR and CRISPR, plus the 2020 Nobel.

**The story**
Every living thing stores instructions in **DNA**, and a **gene** is a stretch of DNA that codes for one protein. If you can cut DNA, add a new piece and join it back, you can give an organism a new trait — this is **recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology**, the foundation of all genetic engineering. To do it you need four tools. **Restriction enzymes** act like scissors that cut DNA only at specific letter-sequences. **DNA ligase** is the glue that joins two cut pieces. A **vector** (a bacterial **plasmid** or a virus called a **bacteriophage**) carries the new gene into a host cell. Finally **PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)** is a photocopier: it doubles a chosen DNA stretch again and again until there are millions of copies (used in RT-PCR COVID tests and forensics). A newer tool, **CRISPR-Cas9**, was borrowed from a bacterial defence system; a short RNA guides the Cas9 protein to an exact spot and cuts, letting scientists edit genes very precisely. Emmanuelle **Charpentier** and Jennifer **Doudna** won the **2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for it.

**Picture it**

| Tool | Everyday name | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Restriction enzyme | Scissors | Cut DNA at a specific sequence |
| DNA ligase | Glue | Join DNA fragments |
| Plasmid / phage | Delivery van | Carry the gene into a cell |
| PCR | Photocopier | Make millions of copies of a DNA piece |

**Terms explained**
- **DNA** = the molecule that stores an organism's instructions.
- **Gene** = a section of DNA coding for one protein.
- **Recombinant DNA** = DNA made by joining pieces from different sources.
- **Vector** = the plasmid or virus that ferries a gene into a host cell.
- **Indel** = a small insertion or deletion of DNA letters.

**Don't confuse**
- **SDN-1 / SDN-2** edits leave **no foreign DNA** (small indels or a tiny template change); **SDN-3** inserts a **large foreign gene** and is therefore treated as a GM/transgenic.
- PCR only **copies** DNA — it does not sequence it or insert it into a cell.

**The three genome-editing categories (SDN = Site-Directed Nuclease)**

| Category | What happens | Foreign DNA? |
|---|---|---|
| SDN-1 | Small insertions/deletions from the cell's own repair, no foreign DNA | No |
| SDN-2 | Edit using a small donor template to introduce defined changes | No (only a tiny template-guided change) |
| SDN-3 | Insertion of a large foreign gene/sequence at a target site | Yes — treated as GM |

**Remember it**
"Cut, glue, carry, copy" = restriction enzyme, ligase, vector, PCR. CRISPR = find-and-edit with an RNA guide.

**TL;DR**
- rDNA technology (joining DNA from different sources) is the basis of genetic engineering.
- Restriction enzymes cut, ligase joins, plasmids/phages carry, PCR amplifies.
- CRISPR-Cas9 edits precisely; Charpentier and Doudna won the 2020 Chemistry Nobel.
- SDN-1/SDN-2 carry no foreign DNA; SDN-3 does and is treated as GM.
keyPoints: Recombinant DNA technology joins DNA from different sources; it is the basis of genetic engineering.
Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sites; DNA ligase joins fragments; plasmids/phages act as vectors.
PCR amplifies a DNA segment into millions of copies (used in RT-PCR COVID tests, forensics).
CRISPR-Cas9 is a precise gene-editing tool; Charpentier and Doudna won the 2020 Chemistry Nobel.
SDN-1 and SDN-2 edits carry no foreign DNA; SDN-3 introduces a foreign gene and is treated as GM.
SDN-1 = small indels by the cell's own repair; SDN-2 = small donor template for defined changes; SDN-3 = large foreign gene inserted at a target site.

items.title: GM crops, GEAC & genome-edited rice (2025)
items.body:
### GM crops, GEAC and genome-edited rice (2025)

**In one line**
India allows only one GM crop in farmers' fields (Bt cotton), keeps others stuck in approvals or courts, but has quietly cleared a new, DNA-foreign-free class of "genome-edited" crops.

**Why it is asked**
The regulator's name and ministry, Bt cotton vs Bt brinjal vs GM mustard status, and the May-2025 genome-edited rice names are recurring, high-value facts.

**The story**
A **GM (genetically modified) crop** carries a gene moved in from another organism. Because that raises safety and ecology questions, every environmental release must be cleared by the **GEAC (Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee)**, which sits under the **MoEFCC (Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change)**, acting under the **Rules of 1989** made under the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**; the **RCGM** under the DBT handles the earlier research and trial stages. Even **confined field trials of GM crops need regulatory clearance** (RCGM/GEAC and state consent) — nothing GM is planted without approval. In practice India has been cautious. **Bt cotton** (cleared 2002) is still the **only GM crop grown commercially**. **Bt brinjal** was approved by GEAC in 2009 but a **moratorium was imposed in 2010 pending further studies and public consultation**, so despite that approval it is **not cultivated commercially** — the moratorium is the reason. **GM mustard (DMH-11)** — a **transgenic hybrid developed by Delhi University's Centre for Genetic Manipulation of Crop Plants** (team led by Deepak Pental) — got a GEAC environmental-release recommendation in 2022, but in 2024 a two-judge **Supreme Court bench split**, so the matter stalled and the Court asked for a national GM policy. Then came a different route: in **May 2025** India released its **first two genome-edited rice varieties — DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala)** from ICAR-IIRR, Hyderabad, and **Pusa DST Rice 1** from ICAR-IARI, New Delhi. Made with **SDN-1/SDN-2 editing** that adds **no foreign DNA**, they are **exempt** from GM biosafety rules and aim at higher yield, drought tolerance and less water and fertiliser.

**Picture it**

| Crop | Status |
|---|---|
| Bt cotton | Only GM crop in commercial cultivation (2002) |
| Bt brinjal | Approved 2009, under moratorium since 2010 |
| GM mustard (DMH-11) | GEAC release nod 2022; Supreme Court split verdict 2024 |
| Genome-edited rice (2025) | DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) and Pusa DST Rice 1; SDN-1/SDN-2, exempt |

**Terms explained**
- **GEAC** = apex body that appraises environmental release of GMOs.
- **Moratorium** = an official hold stopping something indefinitely.
- **Environmental release** = permission to grow the crop in open fields.
- **Genome editing (SDN-1/SDN-2)** = tweaking the plant's own genes without adding foreign DNA.

**Don't confuse**
- **Genome-edited rice** is **not transgenic** — no foreign gene, so it skips GM biosafety rules; GM mustard and Bt crops **are** transgenic.
- GEAC is under the **Environment** ministry, not Agriculture.

**Remember it**
"One in the field (Bt cotton), one on hold (Bt brinjal), one in court (GM mustard), two edited (2025 rice)."

**TL;DR**
- GEAC (under MoEFCC) is the apex regulator; RCGM (DBT) handles research/trials.
- Bt cotton is India's only commercial GM crop; Bt brinjal under 2010 moratorium.
- GM mustard DMH-11: GEAC nod 2022, Supreme Court split verdict 2024.
- First genome-edited rice (May 2025): DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) and Pusa DST Rice 1.
keyPoints: GEAC (under MoEFCC) is the apex regulator for environmental release of GMOs in India.
Bt cotton is India's only commercially cultivated GM crop (approved 2002).
Bt brinjal was approved in 2009 but placed under a moratorium in 2010.
GM mustard DMH-11 got GEAC environmental-release nod in 2022; the Supreme Court gave a split verdict in 2024.
India released its first genome-edited rice varieties — DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) and Pusa DST Rice 1 — in May 2025 using SDN-1/SDN-2.
Confined field trials of GM crops require regulatory clearance (RCGM/GEAC).
DMH-11 was developed by Delhi University's Centre for Genetic Manipulation of Crop Plants (Deepak Pental).
items.source: MoEFCC / GEAC; PIB & ICAR — genome-edited rice, May 2025

items.title: Biotech policy & institutions — BioE3, DBT, BIRAC, BRIC
items.body:
### Biotech policy and institutions — BioE3, DBT, BIRAC, BRIC

**In one line**
India now treats biotechnology as an economic engine: one department runs it (DBT), one body funds start-ups (BIRAC), one merged council does research (BRIC), and one 2024 policy ties it to jobs and the environment (BioE3).

**Why it is asked**
The BioE3 full form and its approval year, and what BRIC actually merged, are clean one-mark facts and also feed a Mains "bioeconomy" answer.

**The story**
The **DBT (Department of Biotechnology)**, under the Ministry of Science and Technology, is India's nodal department for biotech. To turn lab ideas into companies it set up **BIRAC**, a public-sector enterprise that **funds biotech start-ups and innovation**. Research had become scattered across many small institutes, so in **2024** the government created the **BRIC (Biotechnology Research and Innovation Council)** by **merging 14 autonomous DBT institutes** into a single apex society, pooling money and talent. The headline move is the **BioE3 Policy (2024)** — **Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment** — approved by the **Union Cabinet in August 2024**. It pushes **high-performance biomanufacturing**, **biofoundries** and bio-AI hubs across sectors such as bio-based chemicals and enzymes, functional foods, precision biotherapeutics, climate-resilient agriculture, carbon capture, and marine and space biotech. The aim is to shift India toward a **bio-based, circular economy** on a **net-zero** path while creating skilled green jobs.

**Picture it**

| Body / policy | Role |
|---|---|
| DBT | Nodal department for biotechnology |
| BIRAC | Funds biotech start-ups and innovation |
| BRIC (2024) | One society formed by merging 14 DBT institutes |
| BioE3 (2024) | Policy linking biotech to economy, environment, employment |

**Terms explained**
- **Biomanufacturing** = making useful products (chemicals, fuels, medicines) using living cells instead of fossil feedstock.
- **Biofoundry** = an automated facility that designs and tests engineered biology quickly.
- **Circular economy** = reusing and recycling resources instead of "make-use-throw".

**Don't confuse**
- **BIRAC funds**; **BRIC does research**; **DBT governs**. They are not the same body.
- BioE3's third E is **Employment**, not Energy or Education.

**Remember it**
"BioE3 = Economy, Environment, Employment" — three E's, approved 2024.

**TL;DR**
- DBT is the nodal biotech department; BIRAC funds start-ups.
- BRIC (2024) merged 14 DBT institutes into one apex society.
- BioE3 Policy (2024) = Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment.
- It backs biomanufacturing and a bio-based, circular, net-zero economy.
keyPoints: DBT is India's nodal biotech department; BIRAC funds biotech start-ups and innovation.
BRIC (2024) merged 14 DBT autonomous institutes into one apex society.
BioE3 Policy (2024) = Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment, approved by the Union Cabinet.
BioE3 promotes high-performance biomanufacturing, biofoundries and bio-based products.
BioE3 supports India's move toward a bio-based, circular economy and net-zero goals.
items.source: PIB / DBT — BioE3 Policy (2024) and BRIC establishment

items.title: Medical biotech, vaccines & Genome India
items.body:
### Medical biotech, vaccines and Genome India

**In one line**
Biotech reaches medicine through made-in-India vaccines and through the Genome India Project, which is building a reference "map" of Indian DNA for tailored treatment.

**Why it is asked**
"World's first DNA vaccine", the Covaxin platform, and the Genome India targets/funder are frequent single-fact and statement-based questions.

**The story**
During COVID-19 India built vaccines on different platforms. **Covaxin (BBV152)**, from Bharat Biotech with ICMR-NIV, used an **inactivated (killed) virus**. **ZyCoV-D**, from Zydus Cadila, became the **world's first approved DNA vaccine for humans** — needle-free and given into the skin. Beyond vaccines, **gene therapy** repairs disease-causing genes, while **stem cells**, **biosimilars** and **precision (personalised) medicine** are growing fields. The big national effort is the **Genome India Project (GIP)**, launched in **January 2020**, **funded by the Department of Biotechnology (DBT)** and coordinated with the **IISc Centre for Brain Research** and 20-plus institutions. Its goal is to sequence **10,000 Indian genomes** in phase 1 to create an **Indian reference genome** — a **reference database of genetic variation in Indian populations** that captures the country's unusual genetic diversity; completion of the 10,000-genome sequencing was announced in **2025**, opening the door to precision-medicine and disease-prediction research.

**Picture it**

| Vaccine | Platform |
|---|---|
| Covaxin (BBV152) | Inactivated (killed) virus |
| ZyCoV-D | DNA (world's first for humans) |
| Covishield | Viral vector (Oxford-AstraZeneca) |
| Corbevax | Protein subunit |

**Terms explained**
- **Genome** = the complete set of an organism's DNA.
- **Sequencing** = reading the exact order of DNA letters.
- **Reference genome** = a standard map against which individual DNA is compared.
- **Precision medicine** = treatment matched to a person's own genetic make-up.

**Don't confuse**
- **ZyCoV-D is a DNA vaccine**; **Covaxin is an inactivated-virus vaccine** — a common swap.
- Genome India is run by **DBT (science)**, not the health ministry.

**Remember it**
"ZyCoV-D = DNA first; Genome India = 10,000 Indian genomes."

**TL;DR**
- Covaxin = indigenous inactivated-virus COVID vaccine (Bharat Biotech + ICMR).
- ZyCoV-D (Zydus) = world's first approved human DNA vaccine, needle-free.
- Genome India Project (2020, DBT-funded) targets 10,000 Indian genomes.
- 10,000-genome sequencing completion announced in 2025 for precision medicine.
keyPoints: Covaxin is India's indigenous inactivated-virus COVID-19 vaccine (Bharat Biotech + ICMR).
ZyCoV-D by Zydus Cadila is the world's first approved DNA vaccine for humans (needle-free).
Genome India Project (launched 2020, DBT-funded) targets 10,000 Indian genomes in phase 1.
GIP is coordinated with the IISc Centre for Brain Research and 20+ institutions.
Completion of 10,000-genome sequencing under GIP was announced in 2025 for precision medicine.
items.source: PIB / ICMR — COVID-19 vaccines; DBT — Genome India Project

items.title: Nanotechnology — scale, materials & applications
items.body:
### Nanotechnology — scale, materials and applications

**In one line**
Nanotechnology works at the scale of a billionth of a metre, where ordinary materials suddenly gain new and useful powers.

**Why it is asked**
The size of a nanometre, which department runs the Nano Mission, and the properties of graphene, nanotubes and quantum dots are standard science items.

**The story**
A **nanometre (nm) is one-billionth of a metre (10^{-9} m)** — tens of thousands of times thinner than a hair. At this scale a material's **optical, electrical and mechanical properties change**, so the same substance can behave very differently. India's **Nano Mission (2007)**, run by the **DST (Department of Science and Technology)**, funds nanoscience research, infrastructure and trained people. A few star nanomaterials appear again and again: **graphene** is a **single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal (honeycomb) lattice** and a superb conductor; **carbon nanotubes** are rolled carbon with extremely high tensile strength; and **quantum dots** are tiny semiconductor crystals whose glowing colour depends on their size. Applications span **medicine** (targeted drug delivery, imaging, diagnostics), **electronics** (smaller, faster chips and displays), and the **environment** (water-purification membranes, stronger textiles, better catalysts and energy storage). Don't mix the fields, though: **biofertilisers and biopesticides** (living microbes that feed crops or kill pests) belong to **agricultural biotechnology**, not nanotechnology — while **targeted drug delivery** is **nanomedicine** and **water-purification membranes** are a **nanotechnology** application. The flip side is **nanotoxicity** — the possible health and environmental risks of engineered nanoparticles — which remains an active safety concern.

**Picture it**

| Nanomaterial | Key feature |
|---|---|
| Graphene | One-atom-thick carbon; excellent conductor |
| Carbon nanotube | Rolled carbon; very high tensile strength |
| Quantum dot | Semiconductor crystal; colour set by size |

**Terms explained**
- **Nanoscale** = roughly 1 to 100 nanometres.
- **Tensile strength** = how much pulling force a material takes before breaking.
- **Semiconductor** = a material that conducts electricity only partly, used in chips.
- **Nanotoxicity** = harm caused by nanoparticles to health or the environment.

**Don't confuse**
- **Nano Mission is under DST**, while the biotech missions are under DBT.
- Natural nanoparticles (soot, volcanic ash) **do exist** — nanoparticles are not only human-made.

**Remember it**
"Nano = 10^{-9} m; new properties, new uses, new risks (nanotoxicity)."

**TL;DR**
- 1 nanometre = one-billionth of a metre; properties change at the nanoscale.
- India's Nano Mission (2007) is run by the DST.
- Graphene conducts superbly; nanotubes are very strong; quantum dots colour by size.
- Uses: drug delivery, electronics, water purification; nanotoxicity is the concern.
keyPoints: 1 nanometre = one-billionth of a metre; matter shows new properties at the nanoscale.
India's Nano Mission (2007) is run by the Department of Science and Technology (DST).
Graphene is a single layer of carbon; carbon nanotubes have very high tensile strength.
Quantum dots are semiconductor nanocrystals whose emitted colour depends on their size.
Nanotech aids drug delivery, electronics, water purification and textiles; nanotoxicity is a safety concern.
Pairs: targeted drug delivery = nanomedicine; water-purification membranes = nanotechnology; biofertilisers/biopesticides = agricultural biotechnology.

items.title: Bioethics, IPR & Andhra Pradesh ecosystem
items.body:
### Bioethics, IPR and the Andhra Pradesh ecosystem

**In one line**
Powerful biotech needs guard-rails — global treaties on safe movement and fair sharing of genes, a national law against biopiracy — and Andhra Pradesh plugs in through its medtech and life-sciences clusters.

**Why it is asked**
"Match the protocol to its focus" (Cartagena vs Nagoya), the Biological Diversity Act year, and AMTZ's location are reliable one-markers; ethics feeds Mains.

**The story**
Two treaties under the **Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)** set the rules. The **Cartagena Protocol** governs the **safe transboundary movement of living modified organisms (LMOs)** — stopping risky GM material crossing borders unchecked. The **Nagoya Protocol** governs **access to genetic resources and fair, equitable benefit-sharing**, so communities are paid when their biological wealth is used. **Biopiracy** — taking biological resources or traditional knowledge for commercial use without permission — is checked in India by the **Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023)** and the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library. Live ethical debates include GM food safety, patents on life forms and especially **germline editing** (changing genes in human embryos). Regionally, **AMTZ (Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone), Visakhapatnam** is India's first dedicated **medical-devices manufacturing** park, cutting import dependence, built to **promote domestic manufacturing of medical devices**, while **Genome Valley** — a major biotech cluster in the Hyderabad region of neighbouring **Telangana** — anchors life-sciences industry next door.

Patents on biotech inventions fall under the WTO's **TRIPS Agreement** (**Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights**), which sets minimum IPR standards that India's Patents Act follows.

**Picture it**

| Instrument | Focus |
|---|---|
| Cartagena Protocol | Safe transboundary movement of LMOs |
| Nagoya Protocol | Access to genetic resources and benefit-sharing |
| TRIPS Agreement (WTO, 1995) | Trade-related aspects of intellectual property rights (patents, plant varieties) |
| Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023) | Checks biopiracy, implements CBD in India |

**Terms explained**
- **LMO** = living modified organism (a living GM organism).
- **Benefit-sharing** = sharing profits with those who provided the genetic resource.
- **Biopiracy** = unauthorised commercial use of biological resources or traditional knowledge.
- **Germline editing** = editing genes in eggs, sperm or embryos, so changes pass to children.

**Don't confuse**
- **Cartagena = safety of movement; Nagoya = sharing of benefits.** Both are under the CBD.
- AMTZ (medical devices) is in **Visakhapatnam**; Genome Valley is in the **Hyderabad** region.

**Remember it**
"CartageNa = movemeNt; Nagoya = beNefit." AMTZ = medtech, Vizag.

**TL;DR**
- Cartagena Protocol = safe movement of living modified organisms.
- Nagoya Protocol = access and fair benefit-sharing (both under the CBD).
- Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023) checks biopiracy.
- AMTZ Visakhapatnam = India's first medical-devices park; Genome Valley nearby.
keyPoints: Cartagena Protocol governs safe transboundary movement of living modified organisms.
Nagoya Protocol covers access to genetic resources and fair benefit-sharing (both under the CBD).
India's Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023) checks biopiracy and implements CBD obligations.
AMTZ Visakhapatnam is India's first dedicated medical-devices manufacturing park.
Genome Valley near Hyderabad is a major regional biotech/life-sciences cluster.
TRIPS (WTO) = Trade-related aspects of intellectual property rights.
items.source: CBD Secretariat; MoEFCC — Biological Diversity Act; Govt of AP — AMTZ

items.title: Applied Genetics — Barcoding, Inheritance, Bt Cotton & Vaccine Platforms
items.body:
### Applied genetics — barcoding, inheritance, Bt cotton and vaccine platforms

**In one line**
These are the "applied" facts APPSC tests: how DNA tells species apart, why mitochondrial disease comes only from the mother, what Bollgard cotton is, how animals are cloned, and that nanoparticles occur naturally too.

**Why it is asked**
Each line here matches a real statement-based MCQ (DNA barcoding limits, three-parent baby, Bollgard, SCNT/Dolly, natural nanoparticles).

**The story**
**DNA barcoding** identifies a species from a short standard gene region (such as **CO1**); it can tell apart look-alike species and detect undesirable plant or animal material in processed food, but it **cannot judge an organism's age**. It differs from **DNA fingerprinting** (pioneered in India at CCMB Hyderabad by Lalji Singh), which identifies **individuals** for forensics and paternity. **Mitochondrial DNA is inherited entirely from the mother**, so a child can inherit mitochondrial disease only from her; **mitochondrial replacement therapy** around IVF can prevent this — the basis of the **"three-parent baby"**. In farming, **Bollgard I and Bollgard II** are **Bt cotton** technologies (Monsanto) using **Cry** genes (Cry1Ac; Cry2Ab) from *Bacillus thuringiensis* to resist bollworm — **India's only commercially cultivated GM crop**, regulated by **GEAC**. Animals are cloned by **SCNT (Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer)**, which produced **Dolly the sheep (1996)**, and **recombinant vector vaccines** use engineered **bacteria or viruses as carriers**. Finally, **natural nanoparticles exist** (soot, volcanic ash); metallic-oxide nanoparticles are used in **cosmetics and sunscreen**, and some commercial nanoparticles entering the environment can be **unsafe**.

**Picture it**

| Technique | What it identifies / does |
|---|---|
| DNA barcoding | Species (not age); food adulterants |
| DNA fingerprinting | An individual (forensics, paternity) |
| SCNT | Reproductive cloning (Dolly, 1996) |

**Terms explained**
- **CO1 gene** = the standard DNA region used as a species "barcode".
- **Mitochondrial DNA** = DNA in the cell's energy organelles, passed via the egg.
- **Cry gene** = a bacterial gene making a protein toxic to specific insects.
- **SCNT** = putting a body-cell nucleus into an egg to grow a genetic copy.

**Don't confuse**
- **Barcoding = species; fingerprinting = individual.**
- Barcoding **cannot** tell an organism's age — a classic trap.

**Remember it**
"Mother's mitochondria, species barcode, Bt-Bollgard cotton, Dolly by SCNT."

**TL;DR**
- DNA barcoding identifies species and food adulterants but not age.
- Mitochondrial DNA is maternal; replacement therapy prevents transmission.
- Bollgard I/II are Bt cotton (Cry genes); India's only commercial GM crop.
- SCNT cloned Dolly (1996); natural nanoparticles (soot, ash) do exist.
keyPoints: DNA barcoding identifies species and detects adulterants in food but cannot assess an organism's age.
Mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited; mitochondrial replacement therapy (three-parent baby) prevents transmission.
Bollgard I/II are Bt cotton technologies using Cry genes; Bt cotton is India's only commercial GM crop.
GEAC (MoEFCC) regulates GMOs; Cartagena Protocol covers Living Modified Organisms.
SCNT is used for reproductive cloning (Dolly, 1996); recombinant vector vaccines use bacteria/viruses as vectors.
Natural nanoparticles (soot, ash) exist; metallic-oxide nanoparticles are used in cosmetics; some pose nanotoxicity risks.
items.source: DBT/ICAR references; UPSC-standard S&T references (verified Sep 2026)

items.title: Molecular Genetics, the Human Genome & Genetic Disorders
items.body:
## From the double helix to genetic diseases

**In one line:** DNA's four bases pair A–T and G–C, three bases make a codon, the Human Genome Project read all 3 billion letters, and a change in one gene or one chromosome can cause a disorder such as sickle-cell anaemia or Down syndrome.

**Why it is asked:** "which base is found only in RNA", "Down syndrome is caused by", "haemophilia is passed through", "sickle-cell is a point mutation of", "Human Genome Project completed in" and "India's first CAR-T therapy" are standard NCERT-plus-current items.

**The story**

DNA is a **double helix** (Watson and Crick, 1953, using **Rosalind Franklin's** X-ray images). Its bases pair **adenine with thymine** and **guanine with cytosine**; in RNA, **uracil** replaces thymine. The **central dogma** says information flows **DNA → RNA → protein**, and a group of **three bases (a codon)** codes for one amino acid. The **Human Genome Project (1990–2003)** read about **3 billion base pairs** and found only about **20,000–25,000 genes**.

Disorders come in two kinds. **Chromosomal** disorders change the number of chromosomes: **Down syndrome = an extra chromosome 21 (trisomy 21)**, **Klinefelter = XXY (male)**, **Turner = XO (female)**. **Gene (Mendelian)** disorders change one gene: **haemophilia** and **red-green colour blindness** are **X-linked recessive**, so they show mostly in **males**; **sickle-cell anaemia** is **autosomal recessive**, caused by a **point mutation** that swaps **glutamic acid for valine** in haemoglobin; **thalassaemia** reduces haemoglobin production. India's **National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023)** aims to end the disease by **2047**. The first approved CRISPR medicine, **Casgevy (2023)**, treats sickle-cell disease, and **NexCAR19 (2023)** became **India's first indigenous CAR-T cell therapy** for blood cancer.

### Molecular genetics

| Concept | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Base pairing in DNA** | adenine–thymine and guanine–cytosine |
| **Uracil** | base found in RNA in place of thymine |
| **Rosalind Franklin** | X-ray diffraction images that revealed the DNA double helix |
| **Central dogma** | DNA → RNA → protein (Francis Crick) |
| **Codon** | three bases that code for one amino acid |
| **Human Genome Project (1990–2003)** | about 3 billion base pairs; only about 20,000–25,000 genes |
| **Human chromosomes** | 46 (23 pairs): 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes |
| **Point mutation** | change of a single base in DNA |
| **Epigenetics** | changes in gene activity without changing the DNA sequence |

### Genetic disorders

| Disorder | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Down syndrome** | extra chromosome 21 (trisomy 21) |
| **Klinefelter syndrome** | XXY — a male with an extra X chromosome |
| **Turner syndrome** | XO — a female with one X chromosome missing |
| **Haemophilia** | X-linked recessive — blood fails to clot; mostly affects males |
| **Red-green colour blindness** | X-linked recessive — far commoner in males |
| **Sickle-cell anaemia** | autosomal recessive point mutation — glutamic acid replaced by valine in haemoglobin |
| **Thalassaemia** | inherited defect that reduces haemoglobin production |
| **Phenylketonuria** | inborn error — the body cannot break down the amino acid phenylalanine |
| **National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission** | launched July 2023 (Shahdol, Madhya Pradesh) — eliminate the disease by 2047 |
| **Casgevy (2023)** | first approved CRISPR-based medicine — for sickle-cell disease and beta-thalassaemia |
| **NexCAR19 (2023)** | India's first indigenous CAR-T cell therapy for blood cancer (IIT Bombay–ImmunoACT) |

## Don't confuse
- **A–T, G–C in DNA; A–U in RNA.**
- **Down = trisomy 21; Klinefelter = XXY (male); Turner = XO (female).**
- **Haemophilia and colour blindness are X-linked (sex-linked); sickle-cell and thalassaemia are autosomal.**
- **Casgevy** = gene-edited cell therapy (CRISPR); **NexCAR19** = engineered immune cells (CAR-T) for cancer.

**Remember it:** "Down has 3, Turner has 1 X, Klinefelter has XXY."

**TL;DR**
- Double helix 1953 (Franklin's X-rays); central dogma DNA → RNA → protein; codon = 3 bases.
- Human Genome Project 1990–2003: about 3 billion base pairs, about 20,000–25,000 genes.
- Down (trisomy 21), Klinefelter (XXY), Turner (XO); haemophilia X-linked; sickle-cell = valine for glutamic acid.
- Sickle Cell Elimination Mission (2023 → 2047); Casgevy (CRISPR, 2023); NexCAR19 (India's first CAR-T, 2023).
keyPoints: Base pairing in DNA — adenine–thymine and guanine–cytosine.
Uracil — base found in RNA in place of thymine.
Down syndrome — extra chromosome 21 (trisomy 21).
Klinefelter syndrome — XXY — a male with an extra X chromosome.

items.title: Biotechnology Applications — Medicine, Agriculture, Environment & Cloning
items.body:
## What biotechnology actually makes

**In one line:** biotechnology gave the world the first genetically engineered drug (human insulin, 1982), insect-resistant and vitamin-rich crops, oil-eating bacteria, cloned animals, stem-cell therapies and antibody-based diagnostic tests.

**Why it is asked:** "first rDNA drug", "Golden rice is rich in", "first GM food", "first gene therapy was for", "ELISA works on", "India's first cloned buffalo", "techniques used to make transgenic crops" and "what is tissue culture" are NCERT-based PSC staples (syllabus: tissue culture, transgenic organisms, immuno-diagnosis).

**The story**

**Recombinant human insulin** (Humulin, Eli Lilly, **1982**), made in **E. coli**, was the first genetically engineered medicine. The first **gene therapy (1990)** treated a 4-year-old with **ADA (adenosine deaminase) deficiency**. **Monoclonal antibodies** come from **hybridoma** cells (Köhler and Milstein, 1975); **ELISA** detects infection through **antigen–antibody** binding — the core of **immuno-diagnosis** (for example HIV tests).

In farming, **plant tissue culture** grows whole plants from a few cells because every plant cell is **totipotent**; **micropropagation** produces thousands of identical plants, and **meristem culture** gives **virus-free** plants. **Golden rice** is engineered to make **beta-carotene (provitamin A)**; the **Flavr Savr tomato (1994)** was the **first GM food** sold. **RNA interference (RNAi)** silences a pest's gene, as in nematode-resistant tobacco. UPSC (2014) lists **cytoplasmic male sterility and gene silencing** — but **not budding or grafting** — as techniques for making transgenic crops.

In the environment, Ananda **Chakrabarty's oil-eating Pseudomonas "superbug"** became the **first patented living organism (US Supreme Court, 1980)**. In animals, **Rosie (1997)** was a transgenic cow whose milk carried human alpha-lactalbumin, and India's **NDRI Karnal** cloned the buffalo **Garima (2009)**.

### Medical biotechnology

| Product / technique | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Recombinant human insulin (Humulin, 1982)** | first genetically engineered drug — made in E. coli |
| **First gene therapy (1990)** | treated ADA (adenosine deaminase) deficiency |
| **Monoclonal antibodies** | identical antibodies from hybridoma cells (Köhler and Milstein, 1975) |
| **ELISA** | detects infection by antigen–antibody reaction — immuno-diagnosis (e.g. HIV) |
| **Biosimilar** | a near-copy of an approved biological medicine after its patent ends |
| **Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC)** | adult cells reprogrammed to an embryonic-like state — Shinya Yamanaka (2006, Nobel 2012) |
| **Embryonic vs adult stem cells** | embryonic are pluripotent (any cell type); adult are multipotent (limited types) |
| **Cord-blood banking** | stores umbilical-cord stem cells for later blood-disorder treatment |
| **Xenotransplantation** | transplanting animal organs (e.g. gene-edited pig kidneys) into humans |

### Agricultural and environmental biotechnology

| Product / technique | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Totipotency** | ability of a single plant cell to grow into a whole plant — basis of tissue culture |
| **Micropropagation** | tissue culture that yields thousands of identical plants (somaclones) |
| **Meristem culture** | gives virus-free plants (e.g. banana, sugarcane, potato) |
| **Somatic hybridisation** | fusing protoplasts of two species — e.g. the "pomato" |
| **Golden rice** | engineered to make beta-carotene (provitamin A) |
| **Flavr Savr tomato (1994)** | first genetically modified food sold |
| **RNA interference (RNAi)** | silences a pest gene — nematode-resistant tobacco (Meloidogyne incognita) |
| **Techniques for transgenic crops (UPSC 2014)** | cytoplasmic male sterility and gene silencing — not budding or grafting |
| **Bt toxin** | Cry protein from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, toxic to specific insects |
| **Biofertilisers** | Rhizobium (legume root nodules), Azotobacter, Azospirillum, cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc), mycorrhiza |
| **Biopesticides** | Bt, the fungus Trichoderma and baculoviruses (NPV) |
| **Oil-eating "superbug"** | Ananda Chakrabarty's Pseudomonas — first patented living organism (1980) |
| **Bioremediation** | using microbes to clean pollutants such as oil spills |
| **Methanogens** | bacteria (e.g. Methanobacterium) that produce methane in biogas plants |

### Cloned and transgenic animals

| Animal | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Rosie (1997)** | transgenic cow whose milk contained human alpha-lactalbumin |
| **Garima (2009)** | India's first cloned buffalo — NDRI Karnal |
| **Noori (2012)** | world's first cloned Pashmina goat — SKUAST Kashmir |
| **Dolly (1996)** | first mammal cloned from an adult body cell — Roslin Institute, Scotland |

## Don't confuse
- **Insulin (1982)** was the first **rDNA drug**; **Flavr Savr (1994)** the first **GM food**; **ADA deficiency (1990)** the first **gene therapy**.
- **Embryonic stem cells = pluripotent; adult = multipotent; iPSC = reprogrammed adult cells.**
- **Meristem culture → virus-free plants; somatic hybridisation → new hybrids (pomato).**
- **Rhizobium** fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules; **Azotobacter** is free-living.

**Remember it:** "Insulin '82, Gene therapy '90, Tomato '94, Dolly '96."

**TL;DR**
- Medicine: Humulin 1982, ADA gene therapy 1990, monoclonals (hybridoma), ELISA immuno-diagnosis, iPSC (Yamanaka).
- Farming: totipotency → tissue culture, micropropagation, meristem culture; Golden rice (beta-carotene); RNAi; Bt Cry genes.
- Environment: Chakrabarty's Pseudomonas, first patented organism (1980); bioremediation; methanogens.
- Animals: Rosie cow 1997; Garima buffalo 2009 (NDRI); Noori Pashmina goat 2012.
keyPoints: Recombinant human insulin (Humulin, 1982) — first genetically engineered drug — made in E. coli.
First gene therapy (1990) — treated ADA (adenosine deaminase) deficiency.
Totipotency — ability of a single plant cell to grow into a whole plant — basis of tissue culture.
Micropropagation — tissue culture that yields thousands of identical plants (somaclones).
Garima (2009) — India's first cloned buffalo — NDRI Karnal.

items.title: Biotech Institutions, Missions & Laws — the Who, Where and Which Act
items.body:
## The bodies and the rulebook of Indian biotechnology

**In one line:** the Department of Biotechnology (1986) runs a family of research institutes and missions, CSIR adds CCMB and IGIB, and a set of laws decides who may own, patent, test and use genetic material.

**Why it is asked:** "CCMB is located at", "ICGEB has centres in", "the Patents Act section against evergreening", "PPV&FR Act protects", "National Biodiversity Authority HQ", "first patented life form" and "the ART and Surrogacy Acts" are frequent match items; Mains M5-9 asks about IPR in science and technology.

**The story**

The **Department of Biotechnology (DBT)** was carved out of the DST in **1986**; its public enterprise **BIRAC** came in **2012**. Among India's best-known labs are the **National Institute of Immunology (New Delhi)**, the CSIR's **Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB, Hyderabad)** and the **Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics (CDFD, Hyderabad)**. The **International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB)** has centres in **New Delhi, Trieste (Italy) and Cape Town (South Africa)**. India stores biological data at the **Indian Biological Data Centre (IBDC), Faridabad** — the country's first national repository for life-science data.

On the legal side, Section **3(d) of the Patents Act** blocks "evergreening" — new forms of a known medicine cannot be patented unless they work better — which the Supreme Court upheld against Novartis's cancer drug **Glivec in 2013**. The **Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001** protects breeders and farmers' rights to save and sow seed; the **National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai, 2003)** enforces the Biological Diversity Act. The **Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act** and the **Surrogacy (Regulation) Act** (both **2021**) govern IVF clinics and ban commercial surrogacy.

### Institutions and missions

| Body / mission | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Department of Biotechnology (DBT)** | set up in 1986, separated from the DST |
| **BIRAC** | Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council — public enterprise of DBT, set up 2012 |
| **National Institute of Immunology (NII)** | New Delhi — immunology and vaccine research |
| **CCMB (CSIR)** | Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad |
| **CDFD** | Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics, Hyderabad |
| **ICGEB** | International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology — New Delhi, Trieste and Cape Town |
| **Rajiv Gandhi Centre for Biotechnology (RGCB)** | Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala |
| **IGIB (CSIR)** | Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology, New Delhi |
| **NABI** | National Agri-Food Biotechnology Institute, Mohali |
| **Indian Biological Data Centre (IBDC)** | Faridabad — India's first national repository for life-science data (2022) |
| **National Biopharma Mission (2017)** | DBT–BIRAC mission with the World Bank ('Innovate in India', i3) for biopharmaceuticals |
| **Institute of Nano Science and Technology (INST)** | Mohali, Punjab — set up under the Nano Mission |

### Laws, treaties and IPR in biotechnology

| Law / case | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Section 3(d), Patents Act** | bars patents on new forms of known medicines without better efficacy (anti-evergreening) |
| **Novartis v. Union of India (2013)** | Supreme Court refused a patent for the cancer drug Glivec under Section 3(d) |
| **Diamond v. Chakrabarty (1980)** | US Supreme Court allowed the first patent on a living (GM) organism |
| **Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001** | protects plant breeders and farmers' rights to save, use and sell seed |
| **National Biodiversity Authority (2003)** | Chennai — approves access to biological resources under the Biological Diversity Act |
| **Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act, 2021** | regulates IVF clinics and sperm/egg banks |
| **Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021** | bans commercial surrogacy; allows only altruistic surrogacy |
| **Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)** | adopted at the Rio Earth Summit, 1992 — parent of Cartagena and Nagoya |
| **Cartagena Protocol dates** | adopted 2000, in force 2003 |
| **Nagoya Protocol dates** | adopted 2010, in force 2014 |
| **Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL)** | India's database that blocks patents on traditional remedies (turmeric, neem, basmati cases) |
| **He Jiankui (China, 2018)** | created the first gene-edited (CRISPR) babies — condemned and jailed |

## Don't confuse
- **DBT (1986)** governs biotech; **DST** runs the Nano Mission; **CSIR** runs CCMB and IGIB.
- **CCMB** = cell and molecular biology; **CDFD** = DNA fingerprinting service — both in **Hyderabad**.
- **Section 3(d)** stops evergreening of **medicines**; the **PPV&FR Act 2001** covers **plant varieties**.
- **CBD (1992)** is the parent; **Cartagena** = biosafety of LMOs; **Nagoya** = benefit-sharing.

**Remember it:** "3(d) = 'don't dress up old drugs'."

**TL;DR**
- DBT 1986, BIRAC 2012; NII New Delhi; CCMB and CDFD Hyderabad; ICGEB New Delhi–Trieste–Cape Town; IBDC Faridabad.
- Patents Act Sec 3(d) — Novartis/Glivec (2013); Chakrabarty (1980) first patented organism; TKDL fights biopiracy.
- PPV&FR Act 2001; NBA Chennai (2003); ART and Surrogacy Acts 2021; He Jiankui's CRISPR babies (2018).
keyPoints: Department of Biotechnology (DBT) — set up in 1986, separated from the DST.
CCMB (CSIR) — Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad.
Section 3(d), Patents Act — bars patents on new forms of known medicines without better efficacy (anti-evergreening).
Novartis v. Union of India (2013) — Supreme Court refused a patent for the cancer drug Glivec under Section 3(d).

items.title: Nanotechnology — Pioneers, Tools, Products & Risks
items.body:
## Who started nanotech, and what it makes today

**In one line:** Richard Feynman imagined it (1959), new microscopes let scientists see and move atoms (1981), carbon "wonder materials" followed (fullerene 1985, nanotubes 1991, graphene 2004), and today nanotech gives sunscreens, antibacterial silver, nano-fertilisers and drug carriers — alongside health and environmental risks.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC asked twice about nanoparticles (2013 risks, 2022 natural nanoparticles) and once about carbon nanotubes (2020: drug carriers, artificial capillaries, biosensors, biodegradable); "nano urea was made by", "graphene Nobel", "quantum-dot Nobel 2023" and "the lotus effect" are frequent too.

**The story**

**Richard Feynman's 1959 talk "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom"** is seen as the birth of the idea; **Norio Taniguchi** coined the word **"nanotechnology" (1974)**. The **scanning tunnelling microscope (STM, 1981)** let scientists see single atoms. **Fullerene (C60, the "buckyball", 1985)** won the 1996 Chemistry Nobel; **carbon nanotubes** were described by **Sumio Iijima (1991)**; **graphene** was isolated by **Geim and Novoselov (2004, Physics Nobel 2010)**; and **quantum dots** won the **2023 Chemistry Nobel**. Engineering runs **top-down** (carving bulk material smaller) or **bottom-up** (building up from atoms). In India, **IFFCO's Nano Urea (2021)** — billed as the **world's first nano-fertiliser** — and **Nano DAP (2023)** cut fertiliser use. UPSC 2013 listed the worries: nanoparticles can **accumulate in soil and water, enter food chains and trigger free radicals** in cells.

### Pioneers, materials and products

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Richard Feynman (1959)** | "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom" — the idea of nanotechnology |
| **Norio Taniguchi (1974)** | coined the word "nanotechnology" |
| **Scanning tunnelling microscope (1981)** | first instrument to image individual atoms (Nobel 1986) |
| **Fullerene C60 ("buckyball", 1985)** | football-shaped carbon molecule — 1996 Chemistry Nobel |
| **Carbon nanotubes (1991)** | described by Sumio Iijima — rolled sheets of graphene |
| **Graphene (2004)** | isolated by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov — 2010 Physics Nobel |
| **Quantum dots** | discovery and synthesis won the 2023 Chemistry Nobel (Bawendi, Brus, Ekimov) |
| **Carbon nanotube uses (UPSC 2020)** | drug and antigen carriers, artificial blood capillaries, biochemical sensors; they are biodegradable |
| **Top-down vs bottom-up** | top-down carves bulk material smaller; bottom-up builds from atoms and molecules |
| **Nano-silver** | antibacterial coating in dressings, textiles and water filters |
| **Titanium dioxide and zinc oxide nanoparticles** | transparent UV blockers in sunscreens and cosmetics |
| **Lotus effect** | nano-rough water-repelling surfaces that clean themselves |
| **IFFCO Nano Urea (2021)** | world's first nano-fertiliser; IFFCO Nano DAP followed in 2023 |
| **Nanoparticle risks (UPSC 2013)** | accumulate in soil and water, enter food chains, trigger free-radical damage |

## Don't confuse
- **Feynman = the idea (1959); Taniguchi = the word (1974).**
- **Fullerene (C60, 1985) ≠ nanotube (1991) ≠ graphene (2004)** — all carbon, different shapes.
- **Graphene Nobel = Physics 2010; quantum dots Nobel = Chemistry 2023; fullerene Nobel = Chemistry 1996.**
- **Nano Urea** is a liquid nano-fertiliser sprayed on leaves — it is **not** a GM product.

**Remember it:** "Feynman dreamed, Taniguchi named, Iijima rolled, Geim peeled."

**TL;DR**
- Feynman 1959; Taniguchi 1974; STM 1981; C60 1985; nanotubes 1991; graphene 2004 (Nobel 2010); quantum dots Nobel 2023.
- Carbon nanotubes: drug carriers, artificial capillaries, biosensors, biodegradable (UPSC 2020).
- Products: nano-silver, TiO2/ZnO sunscreens, lotus-effect coatings, IFFCO Nano Urea (2021) and Nano DAP (2023).
- Risks: accumulation, food-chain entry, free radicals.
keyPoints: Richard Feynman (1959) — "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom" — the idea of nanotechnology.
Fullerene C60 ("buckyball", 1985) — football-shaped carbon molecule — 1996 Chemistry Nobel.

items.title: Vaccine Platforms & Indian Biotech Vaccines
items.body:
## How a vaccine is built — the platform

**In one line:** a vaccine is classified by its platform — live-attenuated, inactivated, subunit, toxoid, viral-vector, mRNA or DNA — and India has firsts in several of them (ZyCoV-D DNA, iNCOVACC nasal, Cervavac HPV, GEMCOVAC mRNA).

**Why it is asked:** "which vaccine uses messenger RNA", "first intranasal COVID vaccine", "India's first indigenous HPV vaccine" and "recombinant vector vaccines use bacteria and viruses" are platform questions that sit between biotech and health.

**The story**

**Live-attenuated** vaccines use a weakened germ (oral polio, measles, BCG); **inactivated** vaccines use a killed one (Covaxin, injectable polio). **Subunit** vaccines carry only a piece of the germ, often made by recombinant DNA — the **hepatitis B vaccine** was the first such recombinant vaccine. **Toxoid** vaccines use a disabled toxin (tetanus, diphtheria). **Viral-vector** vaccines put the germ's gene into a harmless carrier virus (Covishield, Sputnik V). **mRNA** vaccines give the body instructions to make the antigen itself (Pfizer, Moderna; India's **GEMCOVAC** by Gennova). **DNA** vaccines carry a gene ring (plasmid) — **ZyCoV-D** was the world's first for humans. India also made its **first intranasal COVID vaccine, iNCOVACC (Bharat Biotech, 2022)**, and the **first indigenous HPV vaccine, Cervavac (Serum Institute, 2022)** against cervical cancer.

### Platforms and examples

| Platform | How / example |
|---|---|
| **Live-attenuated** | weakened live germ — oral polio, measles, BCG |
| **Inactivated** | killed germ — Covaxin, injectable polio (IPV) |
| **Subunit / recombinant protein** | only a piece of the germ — hepatitis B (first recombinant vaccine), Corbevax |
| **Toxoid** | inactivated toxin — tetanus, diphtheria |
| **Viral vector** | harmless carrier virus delivers the germ gene — Covishield, Sputnik V |
| **mRNA** | gives cells instructions to make the antigen — Pfizer, Moderna; India's GEMCOVAC (Gennova) |
| **iNCOVACC (Bharat Biotech, 2022)** | India's first intranasal (nasal-drop) COVID-19 vaccine |
| **Cervavac (Serum Institute, 2022)** | India's first indigenous HPV vaccine against cervical cancer |
| **Corbevax maker** | Biological E, Hyderabad |

## Don't confuse
- **Covaxin = inactivated; Covishield = viral vector; Corbevax = protein subunit; ZyCoV-D = DNA; GEMCOVAC = mRNA; iNCOVACC = nasal.**
- **Live-attenuated (weakened) ≠ inactivated (killed).**
- **Cervavac** protects against **HPV** (cervical cancer) — not against hepatitis.

**Remember it:** "Killed Covaxin, Carrier Covishield, Chunk Corbevax, Code ZyCoV-D."

**TL;DR**
- Platforms: live-attenuated, inactivated, subunit, toxoid, viral vector, mRNA, DNA.
- Indian firsts: ZyCoV-D (DNA), iNCOVACC (intranasal, 2022), Cervavac (HPV, 2022), GEMCOVAC (mRNA).
- Hepatitis B was the first recombinant (rDNA) vaccine.
keyPoints: Live-attenuated — weakened live germ — oral polio, measles, BCG.
Inactivated — killed germ — Covaxin, injectable polio (IPV).

items.title: For Mains — Biotechnology, Nanotechnology & Genetic Engineering
items.body:
### For Mains — Biotechnology, nanotechnology and genetic engineering

**In one line**
For Paper-5 (Science & Technology), frame biotech as a tool of national development whose promise must be balanced against ethics, biosafety and equity.

**Why it is asked**
The syllabus clause reads "Biotechnology & Nanotechnology — applications, ethics, genetic engineering, immuno-diagnosis" and "IPR in Science & Technology; promotion of science in AP & India", so answers must weigh benefit against regulation.

**The story**
Mains questions here are rarely "what is CRISPR"; they ask you to **evaluate** — the regulatory debate on GM/genome-edited crops, whether BioE3 can build a bioeconomy, or the ethics of gene editing. Organise by dimensions and quote concrete evidence.

**Picture it**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Applications | GM/genome-edited crops, vaccines (Covaxin, ZyCoV-D), gene therapy, nano drug-delivery |
| Significance | Food security, health self-reliance, bioeconomy, green jobs |
| Institutions/policy | DBT, BIRAC, BRIC (2024), BioE3 (2024), Nano Mission (2007) |
| Ethics/limitations | Biosafety data, germline editing, biopiracy, GM-seed dependence |
| Regulation | GEAC (MoEFCC), RCGM (DBT), Cartagena & Nagoya Protocols, Biological Diversity Act 2002 |
| Way forward | Transparent participatory GM policy, labelling, public-sector R&D, strong IPR |

**Facts to quote**
- Genome-edited rice (May 2025): **DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala)**, **Pusa DST Rice 1** (SDN-1/SDN-2, no foreign DNA, exempt).
- **GM mustard DMH-11** — Supreme Court **split verdict, 2024**, directing a national GM policy.
- **BioE3 Policy, 2024**; **BRIC, 2024** (merged 14 DBT institutes); **Genome India** 10,000 genomes (2025).
- AP angle: **AMTZ, Visakhapatnam** (first medical-devices park) and the **Genome Valley** cluster.

**Terms explained**
- **Immuno-diagnosis** = detecting disease using antibody-antigen reactions (e.g. ELISA, rapid kits).
- **Bioeconomy** = economic activity based on biological resources and biomanufacturing.

**Use in answers**
- Example: cite the 2024 GM-mustard split verdict to argue for a clear national policy.
- Quote: "Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment" to frame BioE3.
- Diagram idea: a cycle — research (Genome India) to institutions (BRIC/BIRAC) to industry and jobs (BioE3).

**TL;DR**
- Argue benefit vs biosafety/ethics, not plain definitions.
- Anchor with GEAC/RCGM, Cartagena/Nagoya and the Biological Diversity Act.
- Quote BioE3, BRIC, genome-edited rice (2025), Genome India.
- Bring the AP angle: AMTZ Visakhapatnam and Genome Valley.
keyPoints: Mains (Paper-5) asks you to evaluate benefit vs biosafety, ethics and equity, not define terms.
Regulators to quote: GEAC (MoEFCC), RCGM (DBT); treaties: Cartagena, Nagoya; law: Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
Flagship evidence: BioE3 (2024), BRIC (2024, 14 institutes merged), Genome India (10,000 genomes, 2025).
Recent case law: GM mustard DMH-11 Supreme Court split verdict (2024) directed a national GM policy.
AP angle: AMTZ Visakhapatnam (first medical-devices park) and the Genome Valley cluster.
Way forward: transparent participatory GM policy, labelling, public-sector R&D and strong IPR.
